content: Studies investigating the impact of mass drug administration (MDA) on malaria in areas with moderate to high transmission have shown mixed results. In The Gambia and Zambia, data from cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) revealed that within one to three months after MDA, the prevalence of Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia might be higher compared to control groups, but the confidence intervals (CIs) included no significant effect (relative risk [RR] 1.76, 95% CI 0.58 to 5.36; low-certainty evidence). However, the incidence of parasitemia was likely reduced (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.92; moderate-certainty evidence), and the incidence of confirmed malaria illness may have been substantially lower, though the CIs again included no significant effect (rate ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.04 to 4.42; low-certainty evidence). At four to six months post-MDA, there was little to no effect on P. falciparum parasitemia prevalence (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.56; moderate-certainty evidence), and no sustained effect on parasitemia incidence was observed (rate ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.50). In areas with very low to low malaria transmission, seven studies conducted in Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Vietnam, Zambia, and Zanzibar evaluated the effects of multiple rounds of MDA on P. falciparum. Within one month after MDA, parasitemia prevalence was reduced (RR 0.12, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.52; low-certainty evidence). At one to three months post-MDA, both parasitemia incidence (rate ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.55; moderate-certainty evidence) and prevalence (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.41; low-certainty evidence) were reduced. However, the effect on confirmed malaria incidence was uncertain due to low absolute rates and very low-certainty evidence (rate ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.12 to 2.73). Over time, the relative reductions in P. falciparum prevalence diminished, with RR 0.63 (95% CI 0.36 to 1.12) at four to six months, RR 0.86 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.36) at seven to twelve months, and varying estimates of longer-term effects, such as RR 0.82 (95% CI 0.20 to 3.34) at 13 to 18 months and RR 1.25 (95% CI 0.25 to 6.31) at 31 to 36 months in one study. For Plasmodium vivax, five studies from Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, and Vietnam assessed the impact of MDA. One month after MDA, P. vivax prevalence was reduced (RR 0.18, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.40; low-certainty evidence). At one to three months post-MDA, prevalence was further reduced (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.24; low-certainty evidence). However, this reduction was not sustained over time, with RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.95) at four to six months and RR 1.12 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.32) at seven to twelve months. Longer-term effects were similarly inconsistent, with RR 0.81 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.48) at 13 to 18 months and RR 1.20 (95% CI 0.44 to 3.29) at 31 to 36 months in one study. Non-randomized controlled before-and-after (CBA) studies conducted in moderateto high-transmission areas (Burkina Faso, Kenya, and Nigeria) showed reductions in P. falciparum parasitemia prevalence during MDA (difference-in-differences [DiD] range: -15.8 to -61.4 percentage points). However, the effects varied at one to three months post-MDA (DiD range: 14.9 to -41.1 percentage points). In conclusion, in moderateto high-transmission settings, no significant or sustained reductions in P. falciparum parasitemia prevalence were observed within six months after MDA. In very lowto low-transmission settings, initial reductions in parasitemia prevalence and incidence for both P. falciparum and P. vivax were observed for up to three months, but these effects were not sustained beyond four months. Absolute risks in both intervention and control groups were generally low, and no studies provided evidence of complete interruption of malaria transmission.
